### Sixth Saturday of the Great Fast: Lazarus [Saturday]
*Note.*
The Service of this Feast is of the lesser rank, and only at Matins from the Canon downwards is it of the greater rank; yet even before the Canon it has certain elements of the Resurrection Service; namely, after the 2nd Kathisma, that is, after the Evlogitaria (*Neporóchni*), it has **"The angelic assembly"** (*А҆́нгельскїй собо́ръ*), and after the 2nd Sessional Hymn **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** (*Воскресе́нїе Хрїсто́во ви́дѣвше*), and before the Exaposteilarion: **"Holy is the Lord our God"** (*Свѧ́тъ Госпо́дь Бо́гъ на́шъ*) thrice.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Modern Chant Preservation and the Galician Oral Samohlasen Tradition
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In reality, an immense role in this process belongs to the parish cantor (*diak*) and cantor-teacher (*diako-uchytel*)—a role that is all too infrequently emphasized in our contemporary era. The responsibility of the church singer is profound in preserving tradition: not only in terms of whom he trains to sing, but fundamentally *what* he teaches, what musical foundation he selects, and what he passes down to succeeding generations.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. Staves 7-10 contain Ode 6 Troparion 2 with red initial 'Р': 'Разрѣшены своя оузники сїѡне...'. typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Palm Sunday[^566]
All according to the general Typikon of a Master Feast with Vigil, without Afterfeast. It has all its proper texts, and at the Liturgy Antiphons and the Introit (*Vhódnoje*). However, before the Troparion of Palm Sunday, we sing yesterday's Troparion of Lazarus; only after the Great Doxology do we sing the Troparion of Lazarus alone.

#### At Great Vespers

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L736–L739): ### Palm Sunday[^566] All according to the general Typikon of a Master Feast with Vigil, without Afterfeast. It has all its proper texts, and at the Liturgy Antiphons and the Introit (*Vhódnoje*). However, before the Troparion of Palm Sunday, we sing yesterday's Troparion of Lazarus; only after the Great Doxology do we sing the Troparion of Lazarus alone. #### At Great Vespers

typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Palm Sunday[^566]
All according to the general Typikon of a Master Feast with Vigil, without Afterfeast. It has all its proper texts, and at the Liturgy Antiphons and the Introit (*Vhódnoje*). However, before the Troparion of Palm Sunday, we sing yesterday's Troparion of Lazarus; only after the Great Doxology do we sing the Troparion of Lazarus alone.

#### At Great Vespers

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

manuscript_witnesses.red_text: ВЪ СТЫИ ВЕЛИКЇЙ ПОНЕДѢЛОКЪ . ТРО, ГЛА, И҃.
manuscript_witnesses.incipit_diplomatic: Се женихъ грядетъ во полунощи и блаженъ рабъ єгоже ѡбрящетъ бдяща
manuscript_witnesses.incipit_reconstructed: Се, Женихъ грядетъ въ полунощи, и блаженъ рабъ, єгоже ѡбрящетъ бдяща: недостоинъ же паки, єгоже ѡбрящетъ унывающа. Блюди убо душе моя, не сномъ отяготися, да не смерти предасися, и царствія внѣ затворишися: но воспряни зовущи: Святъ, Святъ, Святъ єси Боже, Богородицею помилуй насъ.
manuscript_witnesses.musical_paleography: Kyivan square notation on red-ruled 5-line staves; C-clef on 3rd line. Opens on f. 439v staff 1 beneath monumental cinnabar display heading, spanning staves 1–6 and concluding across f. 440r staves 1–3 (9 staves total). Melismatic cadence at final Trinitarian doxology and Marian invocation.

Captures the urgent nocturnal vigilance of Great Week.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Matins Chants in Ukrainian Irmologia of the 17th–18th Centuries
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.
scholarly_summaries.verbatim_source: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

provenance.verbatim_source: "physical_landmarks": "Opening spread of f. 422v (left) and f. 423r (right, modern pencil foliation '423', earlier '421' crossed out). 7 red-ruled 5-line staves per page (14 staves total). On f. 423r, staff 5 opens with cinnabar rubric: 'СТЇХИРА . НАГРОБНАА . ВЄЛИ[КИЙ] • ПАТОКЪ • ПОЄМА •' followed by cinnabar initial 'С' and chant: 'Слава ѿцꙋ ї снꙋ ї с҃томꙋ дꙋху, и нынѣ и присно и во вѣ' (Tone 5 Doxastikon of the Shroud / Epitaphios).",

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L879–L881): ### Royal Hours In the Cathedral Church they are sung at the 10th hour of the morning, together with the Typika (*Obidnytsia*) and with Vespers.[^603] We sing all things according to the Typikon of the Royal Hours of the Paramony of the Nativity of Christ, here on p. 181. However, since the Tomb is placed before the Royal Doors, the Analogion of the Gospel is placed a little below it, while the Analogion of the other Readings is placed still lower than this. And all things which at the Paramony of the Nativity the sacred ministers say before the Royal Doors, here they say before the Tomb; but they do not cense the Tomb, because until now there is nothing within it.

typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Royal Hours
In the Cathedral Church they are sung at the 10th hour of the morning, together with the Typika (*Obidnytsia*) and with Vespers.[^603] We sing all things according to the Typikon of the Royal Hours of the Paramony of the Nativity of Christ, here on p. 181. However, since the Tomb is placed before the Royal Doors, the Analogion of the Gospel is placed a little below it, while the Analogion of the other Readings is placed still lower than this. And all things which at the Paramony of the Nativity the sacred ministers say before the Royal Doors, here they say before the Tomb; but they do not cense the Tomb, because until now there is nothing within it.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Modern Chant Preservation and the Galician Oral Samohlasen Tradition
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In reality, an immense role in this process belongs to the parish cantor (*diak*) and cantor-teacher (*diako-uchytel*)—a role that is all too infrequently emphasized in our contemporary era. The responsibility of the church singer is profound in preserving tradition: not only in terms of whom he trains to sing, but fundamentally *what* he teaches, what musical foundation he selects, and what he passes down to succeeding generations.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.
scholarly_summaries.verbatim_source: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

provenance.verbatim_source: "physical_landmarks": "Opening spread of f. 425v (left) and f. 426r (right, modern pencil foliation '426' in upper right margin). 7 red-ruled 5-line staves per page (14 staves total). Folio 425v staves 1–7 conclude 'Тебе ѡдѣющагося' ('...или какими плащаницами обвию... величаю страсти Твоя... слава Тебѣ'). Folio 426r opens at staff 1 with cinnabar rubric: 'Сїє поєтся въ великую субботу' followed by cinnabar initial 'В' and chant: 'Величаемъ тя, Живодавче Христе, и почитаемъ погребенїє' (Stasis 1 of the Epitaphios Megalynaria / Holy Saturday Matins), continuing through staves 1–4. Staff 5 opens with cinnabar initial 'Д' and chant: 'Достойно єсть величати тя, Жизнодавца, на крестѣ руцѣ простершаго' (Stasis 2 of the Megalynaria), continuing through staves 5–7.",

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.
